source_solutions.independent_solution: A mechanical wave is a disturbance or oscillation propagating through an elastic medium by interactions between its particles. A single particle's periodic motion alone is not a wave: the disturbance must travel to other positions.
source_solutions.basis: n38 blocks 0, 5, 6, 8 distinguish particle motion from disturbance propagation.

source_solutions.independent_solution: In a transverse wave the particles oscillate perpendicular to the direction of propagation; a wave on an elastic cord, or the sideways-driven spring-connected ball chain, is an example. In a longitudinal wave they oscillate parallel to propagation; the along-chain-driven spring-connected balls produce traveling compressions and rarefactions. Each example must be paired with the correct direction relationship, not classified from the shape of a curve.

The disturbance propagates while the medium's particles oscillate locally about equilibrium instead of accompanying the disturbance down the medium. Elastic forces transfer the oscillatory disturbance, and thus mechanical energy, onward; wave motion is not bulk transport of the medium. The driven steady outgoing model has a common frequency and downstream phase delays.
source_solutions.basis: n38 blocks 5, 6, 8 and n39 block 6; energy transfer follows from work by the elastic coupling.

source_solutions.independent_solution: Wavelength is the smallest positive spatial separation along propagation between two points with the same oscillation phase. Same phase requires the same displacement and same stage/direction of motion, not merely equal displacement at one instant. In Figure 70 balls 1 and 13, 2 and 14, and 3 and 15 are separated by one wavelength. Balls 1 and 7 are separated by half a wavelength and are in antiphase.
source_solutions.basis: n39 blocks 0 and 2; full Figure 70 e and f.

source_solutions.independent_solution: A wave travels one wavelength in one period, so v=lambda/T=lambda*nu, with nu=1/T. At fixed vibration frequency v is proportional to lambda; without holding frequency fixed, wavelength alone does not determine speed. This relation applies to both transverse and longitudinal waves. Wave propagation speed is distinct from an individual particle's varying oscillation velocity.

Figure 70 e marks one wavelength from ball 1 to ball 13: twelve equal adjacent gaps, not thirteen. Thus adjacent equilibrium positions differ by lambda/12. A full wavelength corresponds to 2*pi radians, hence the adjacent-ball phase-difference magnitude is 2*pi/12=pi/6=30 degrees, equivalent to a downstream time lag T/12. n38's quarter-period spacing is between successive panels, not adjacent balls. Balls 1 and 7 have pi phase difference over six gaps, an independent cross-check.
